To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the liver of the TPN-adapated animal is unresponsive to the hyperinsulinemic clamp.
the liver is unresponsive to insulin in the TPN adapted state, and that infection impairs this response.
the liver of TPN-adapt dogs is insulin-resistant and that an infection further impairs the insulin responsiveness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism.
the effects of infection on hepatic glucose metabolism in the presence of hyperinsulinemia and hyperglycemia.
the regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism in the normal state and under conditions of stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TPN-adaptive changes to the liver do not alter the response of the liver to the infection-induced increase of insulin.
the infection-induced impairment in hepatic insulin action is not a consequence of the adaptation to TBN.
the liver of the TPN-adapated dog is not sensitive to insulin, and infection further reduces that sensitivity, resulting in impaired NHGU.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
infection-induced hyperinsulinemia sustains NHGU in TPN, but further increments in insulin do not increase NHGU.
the infection-induced hyperinsulinemia does not improve the impaired NHGU and glycolysis seen with infection in the TPN-treated animal.
the infection-induced increase of insulin in the hypermetabolic state does not further augment hepatic glucose uptake and that the liver may be insulin-resistant in this setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
infection impairs insulin-dependent NHGU during TPN.
the TPN-adaptive state is characterized by a blunted responsiveness to insulin, and the infection-induced increase of insulin is insufficient to overcome this impairment.
in the TPN state, liver glucose metabolism is unresponsive to further increases in insulin, and infection further impairs that responsiveness.
